title: Checks that keep infra safe

story: An agent opens a pull request in the infrastructure repo. It changes the module for the runs bucket, the S3 bucket where every run keeps its transcript, and the diff is short. CI is green, because CI in that repo only checks formatting. Hidden in the change are three small things: a security group rule that opens port 22 to the whole internet "for debugging", a bucket with no block on public access, and a new retention_days variable that nothing uses, so transcripts would be kept forever instead of 30 days.
A tired reviewer approves, and the next apply makes all three real. A revert can change the code back later, but it cannot change back what happened in between.
hook.question: What can check an infrastructure change before anyone applies it, and why must the one who applies it always be a person?

read.h: Four checks that need no keys
p: Most mistakes in HCL can be found by reading the files, without any cloud account, which means the checks can run on every push, even on an agent's branch. They come in four layers, and each one catches what the one before it cannot see.

tofu fmt -check only looks at layout. tofu validate checks meaning: types, references to things that exist, required arguments. It is tsc for HCL, and with init -backend=false it needs no state and no credentials. But validate only knows the provider's schema, not your intentions. tflint adds rules on top: an input variable that is declared but never used, a missing version constraint, and with its AWS ruleset an instance type that does not exist, such as m8i.2xlage. In the story, tflint is the check that would have asked why retention_days is never used.

The fourth layer looks for risky settings. trivy config, and checkov, which does the same job with its own rules, know what an open security group or a public bucket looks like and report each one with an ID and a severity, such as AWS-0107 (HIGH): Security group rule allows unrestricted ingress from any IP address. Our CI runs trivy and fails on HIGH and CRITICAL findings. One scanner is enough, and running two mostly doubles the noise.

code.file: what infrastructure CI runs on every push
code.text:
# 1. Layout: the same formatting everywhere (exit 3 and a file list if not)
tofu fmt -check -recursive
terragrunt hcl format --check

# 2. Meaning: types, references, required arguments (like tsc for HCL)
tofu init -backend=false && tofu validate

# 3. Rules the language does not know: unused variables, bad instance types
tflint --recursive

# 4. Risky settings: open security groups, public or unencrypted buckets
trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL modules/ terraform/ multi_tenant/

notes.text: This and the next line are all the repo's CI checked before these checks were added.
-backend=false: no state and no cloud keys. Only the provider is downloaded.
tflint reads .tflint.hcl at the repo root to know which rulesets to load.
Scans the HCL files only. Nothing is planned and no AWS call is made.

read.see:
$ trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --quiet modules/   (the module from the story)
Failures: 6 (HIGH: 6, CRITICAL: 0)
AWS-0086 (HIGH): No public access block so not blocking public acls
AWS-0087 (HIGH): No public access block so not blocking public policies
AWS-0091 (HIGH): No public access block so not blocking public acls
AWS-0093 (HIGH): No public access block so not restricting public buckets
AWS-0107 (HIGH): Security group rule allows unrestricted ingress from any IP address.
AWS-0132 (HIGH): Bucket does not encrypt data with a customer managed key.

p: validate is the check you will meet most often, because it runs in a second. Rename a variable in one place and forget the other, and it stops with Reference to undeclared input variable, the line, and the name it could not find. It does not know whether the value is sensible: a warm pool of 50 or an instance type with a typo passes validate. That is what validation blocks in the module (lesson p4-3) and tflint are for.

Some findings are accepted for a while. The runs bucket, for example, might wait one more PR for its own encryption key. trivy reads a .trivyignore file with one finding ID per line, and we add two rules to it: a comment above each line that names an owner and a reason, and an expiry date, after which the finding fails again and someone must decide again. An ignore without an owner is how a temporary exception becomes permanent.

The checks' own files are a target too. If an agent could add AWS-0107 to .trivyignore, it could make its own open security group pass. So the check workflows, .tflint.hcl and .trivyignore are protected paths: an agent's change to them is refused, and a person who did not ask for the work must approve any PR at all. Agents never change the checks they are judged by.

code.text:
# Every line: who owns it, why it is acceptable, and until when.
# owner=devops reason=the runs bucket gets its own KMS key in the next PR
AWS-0132 exp:2026-12-31

notes.text: Who decided, and why, written where the next reader will look.
After this date the finding fails CI again.

read.h: A plan that can only read
p: Static checks cannot tell you what a change will do to the real account: whether a VPC gets replaced or a bucket is renamed. Only a plan can, and a plan needs to read the account. So the pull request workflow plans each changed unit with its own role, TerraformPlanRole, in every account. It has AWS's ReadOnlyAccess with an explicit deny on reading data: objects in buckets, secrets, parameters and decryption keys. It can describe the account but change nothing and read nothing secret.

Only pull_request runs of the infrastructure repo can get that role, through OIDC, the way a GitHub Actions run gets short-lived AWS credentials without any stored key (lesson p2-3). Because the role can write nothing, the plan runs with -lock=false, since even a state lock is a write. And it never saves a plan file with -out, because a plan file holds every value in plain text, secrets included. The result is one comment on the PR with each unit's Plan: line and the addresses that change, so the reviewer reads the effect next to the diff.

code.text:
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["terraform/**", "modules/**", "multi_tenant/**"]

permissions: { id-token: write, contents: read, pull-requests: write }

jobs:
  plan:
    runs-on: infrastructure-runner-set
    env:
      TG_ROLE_NAME: TerraformPlanRole # read by account.hcl; never the deployment role here
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@<sha> # pinned by SHA
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::<inf-account>:role/GitHubActionsTerraformPlan
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - name: Plan each changed unit (read-only, no lock, no plan files)
        run: |
          while read -r unit; do
            (cd "$unit" && terragrunt plan -lock=false -input=false -no-color) > "plan-${unit//\//_}.txt" 2>&1 || true
          done < changed-units.txt
      - name: One comment with each unit's Plan line
        run: .github/scripts/post_plan_comment.sh changed-units.txt

notes.text: Pull requests only. There is no workflow_dispatch and no apply job anywhere in this file.
account.hcl reads this variable to pick the role to assume, so plans can never use the role that applies.
The OIDC role trusts only pull_request runs of RhinoHealth/infrastructure.
-lock=false because the role cannot write a lock; no -out because a plan file holds secrets.

read.h: Why the last step is a person
p: Every check above can be wrong or incomplete, and an apply changes the real world at once. A git revert restores the code, but it does not un-delete a database, and it does not undo what someone did through an open port in the meantime. So the rule for infrastructure is the same as for merging: agents may write HCL, run every check and read the plan comment, but they never apply, destroy, sync or dispatch a workflow. A person reads the plan, starting with the destroys and replacements, and applies.

This rule does not depend on an agent's instructions, because nothing an agent holds can apply. No agent has a role that can write to any account, the PR workflow can only plan, and the GitHub App that agents use has no permission to change or dispatch workflows. An agent that is fooled into trying simply has no button to press.

deeper.h: Go deeper: why plans skip some units at first
p: Some units call more than AWS. Units for tools on the internal cluster also read secrets from Vault and talk to the Kubernetes API. A read-only plan of those needs a read-only Vault role and a view-only Kubernetes access entry. Until those exist, the PR workflow skips such units and says so, and the author still runs those plans by hand and pastes them into the PR.

lab.title: Catch a bad infra PR before a person applies it
needs: OpenTofu (for tofu fmt; nothing is planned or applied, and the aws provider is never downloaded).
trivy (trivy --version). Without it, use the aquasec/trivy Docker image with the same arguments.
Docker, for tflint (ghcr.io/terraform-linters/tflint) and, optionally, checkov (bridgecrew/checkov).
lab.goal: Run the four key-free checks on the bad runs-bucket module from the story, fix what they find, and keep one exception with an owner and an expiry.

guess.q: The module from the story has a public-by-default bucket, port 22 open to the world and an unused retention_days variable. Which check finds the unused variable?

options.text: tofu fmt -check, because it reads every line.
options.why: fmt only cares about layout: spaces, alignment, indentation. An unused variable is perfectly formatted.

options.text: trivy config, because it scans the whole module.
options.why: trivy looks for risky settings. An unused variable is not risky by itself; it is a sign that something was forgotten.
tflint knows rules the language does not enforce, such as "declared but never used". Here it points straight at the missing lifecycle rule.

follow.say: Make the lab folder and paste this block, because it writes the module from the story exactly as the agent's PR had it. Nothing here is ever planned or applied.
Start with layout, because it is the cheapest check and CI already runs it. Then let fmt fix it.
Run tflint, because it knows rules that the language and fmt do not.

follow.say: Ask the question CI asks: does this fail the build? --exit-code 1 turns findings into a failing exit code.

lab.build: Make the module pass. Add required_version = ">= 1.10" to the terraform block. Add an aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block for the bucket with all four flags set to true, and an aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration with one enabled rule whose expiration uses var.retention_days. Remove the ingress block from the security group (the sandboxes need no ingress at all). One finding stays: the bucket's own KMS key comes in the next PR. Accept it in .trivyignore with an owner, a reason and an expiry date. Then run fmt, tflint and trivy with --exit-code 1 again.
checks: tflint prints nothing and exits 0: retention_days is now used.
trivy config --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --quiet modules/ without the ignore file shows exactly one finding, AWS-0132.
With your .trivyignore, trivy --exit-code 1 exits 0, and the ignore line has an owner, a reason and an exp: date.
The security group has no ingress block at all.

solution.file: modules/runs-bucket/main.tf, plus .trivyignore from the Understand step

lab.fix: A second agent PR "fixes CI" for a module like this one. trivy is green, yet checkov still reports CKV_AWS_24 for port 22. Recreate it: put the ingress block for port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0 back into the security group, and add a bare line AWS-0107 to the end of .trivyignore. trivy --exit-code 1 now exits 0. Find why, and fix it properly: remove the ingress block and the ignore line, and explain which wall should have refused this PR before any person saw it.
explain: Which of the four checks would have caught each of the three problems in the story, and why can none of them run apply?
Why does the PR plan run with a read-only role, -lock=false and no -out plan file?
An agent is fooled into trying to apply a change. What stops it, and why does that not depend on the agent's instructions?
lab.done: fmt, tflint and trivy (--exit-code 1) all pass on your fixed module, the one remaining exception has an owner, a reason and an expiry, and you can say which wall refuses an agent's edit to .trivyignore.

check.q: tofu validate passes on a module whose security group allows port 22 from 0.0.0.0/0. Why didn't it complain?

options.text: validate checks that the HCL is correct (types, references, required arguments), not whether a setting is safe.
options.why: That is the job of a misconfiguration scanner such as trivy config. The layers catch different things, so you need all of them.

options.text: validate only runs on Terragrunt units, not on modules.
options.why: CI runs validate on every module. It simply has no rules about safety.

options.text: Because 0.0.0.0/0 is a valid CIDR, so it is safe.
options.why: Valid is not the same as safe. 0.0.0.0/0 means the whole internet.

check.q: Why does the PR plan workflow never use tofu plan -out=plan.tfplan?

options.text: Because plan files are too large to upload.
Because a plan file holds every value in plain text, secrets included, and a PR workflow should leave nothing like that behind.
options.why: The comment carries the summary and the full text stays in the job log of a private repo. A saved plan file would be one more place for secrets to leak.

options.text: Because -out makes the plan apply automatically.
options.why: -out only saves the plan. Applying it is a separate command, which this workflow never runs.

check.q: An agent opens an infrastructure PR, every check is green, and the plan comment says 0 to destroy. Who applies it, and why?

options.text: The agent, because every check passed.
options.why: Checks can be wrong or incomplete, and apply changes the real world at once. Agents never apply; nothing they hold can.

options.text: Nobody needs to: the plan workflow applies green PRs.
options.why: The plan workflow can only plan. There is no apply step and no dispatch in it.

options.text: A person, after reading the plan, because an apply cannot be taken back with a revert and the walls give agents no way to apply.
options.why: Agents write HCL and read plans; a person who did not ask for the work approves the PR, and a person applies.

p: Today the infrastructure repo's CI, terrugrunt-lint.yml, runs only tofu fmt -check and terragrunt hcl format --check, and plans are pasted into PRs by hand. A new terraform-checks.yml adds validate on every modules/* folder, tflint with the aws and google rulesets from a root .tflint.hcl, and trivy config over modules/, terraform/ and multi_tenant/: advisory for two weeks while Security goes through the findings, then failing on new HIGH and CRITICAL ones, with an owner and a reason on every .trivyignore line.

Each account gets a TerraformPlanRole (ReadOnlyAccess plus an explicit deny on data reads), assumed through an OIDC role in the inf account that trusts only pull_request runs of RhinoHealth/infrastructure. terragrunt-plan.yml posts one comment per PR with each changed unit's plan. The check workflows, .tflint.hcl and .trivyignore go on the paths agents may not change.

tickets.why: validate, tflint and trivy config in infrastructure CI, with no cloud keys and owned exceptions.
The read-only TerraformPlanRole per account and the OIDC role only PR runs may assume.
Read-only Terragrunt plans posted on infrastructure PRs; nothing in it can apply.
Locked checks: agent PRs that edit CI, lint or check files are blocked.
The infra upgrade fixer opens exactly the kind of PR these checks must judge.

words.plain: A linter for HCL with rulesets: unused variables, missing version constraints, and with the AWS ruleset, instance types that do not exist.
A scanner that reads Terraform files and reports risky settings, such as open security groups, with an ID and a severity. checkov does the same job.
The list of accepted findings; ours needs an owner, a reason and an expiry date on every line.
TerraformPlanRole: can describe an account but change nothing and read no data, so PR plans are safe to run.
Files such as check workflows and ignore lists that an agent's PR may not change.

review.q: Name the four key-free checks in order and one thing each catches that the previous one does not.
review.a: fmt (layout), validate (types and references), tflint (rules such as unused variables or bad instance types), trivy config (risky settings such as an open security group or a public bucket).

review.q: Write a correct .trivyignore entry for a finding you accept until the end of the year.
review.a: A comment with owner and reason, then the ID with an expiry, for example: # owner=devops reason=KMS key comes in the next PR, then AWS-0132 exp:2026-12-31.

review.q: List what an agent may and may not do in the infrastructure repo.
review.a: May: write HCL, run fmt, validate, tflint and trivy, read the plan comment. May not: apply, destroy, sync, dispatch workflows, or edit the check workflows, .tflint.hcl or .trivyignore.

remember: Let key-free checks and a read-only plan judge every infrastructure change, keep every exception owned and dated, and leave apply to a person.
